title: Examining Food Self‐Sufficiency and Food Security in Nepal Amidst High Rates of Migration
content:
Abstract

The emergence of global food trade has ameliorated food insecurity in several countries as food imports supplement the dietary demands of a country's population. At the same time, migration of agricultural workers can make a country reliant on food imports as it can curtail domestic production. The unprecedented high rates of migration from Nepal have contributed to observed agricultural production decline in the country. In this study we evaluate the food system in Nepal and how domestic food production and trade have evolved from 1990 to 2021 amidst high rates of migration. Using data sets from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), this work primarily analyzes the trends in domestic production and imports of four main cereals (rice, wheat, maize, and millet) as well as pulses and potato. We show that there has been a decline in land used for agriculture in Nepal since the 1990s and an increased use of fertilizers in domestic agriculture suggesting an intensification of domestic food production. Despite rising prices of cereals and a 70% increase in real gross production value over the study period, cereal and pulse self-sufficiency declined by 30% and 45% respectively with outmigration a significant predictor of declining self-sufficiency. We calculated that 53% of both current land and water input would be required to achieve self-sufficiency and doing so would increase total water demand. Our findings highlight the limits to self-sufficiency and emphasize the need for strategies that balance domestic production and trade to strengthen Nepal's food security.
